excerpt: Build Copilot UX components, web parts, extensions, and business solutions with SharePoint Framework and Microsoft 365.
Now, developers can interact remotely with SharePoint data by using any technology that supports REST web requests.
Perform basic CRUD operations on folders and files with the SharePoint REST interface.
Use **PUT** and **MERGE** operations to update existing SharePoint objects.
There are recyclable objects, such as lists, files, and list items, this results in a **Recycle** operation.
The SharePoint Online (and on-premises SharePoint 2016 or later) REST service supports combining multiple requests into a single call to the service by using the OData `$batch` query option.
The client.svc web service handles the HTTP request and serves the appropriate response in either Atom or JSON format.
For SharePoint Online, use SPFx for user interface extensions and Microsoft Entra ID for authentication to external applications.
To figure out if a Microsoft Graph REST API call is backed by SharePoint Online you can add `$whatif` to the end of the query to output the underlying SharePoint URL.
Read-write support for **lists**, **listItems**, and **driveItems**
Read-write support for tenant-level **SharePointSettings**
Address resources by SharePoint ID, URL, or relative path
You can expand references in your URL with the _expand_ query parameter; for example, `?expand=fields`.
Sites can also be addressed by path by using the SharePoint hostname, followed by a colon and the relative path to the site.
The following examples help developers familiar with SharePoint REST v1 API URL patterns adapt their use cases to similar Microsoft Graph API URL patterns.
SharePoint webhooks enable developers to build applications that subscribe to receive notifications on specific events that occur in SharePoint.
SharePoint webhooks provide a simple notification pipeline so that your application can be aware of changes to a SharePoint list without polling the service.
You can use this for validating notifications, tagging different subscriptions, or other reasons.
If an error occurs while sending the notification to your application, SharePoint retries up to 5 times to deliver the notification.

A former user says every time they used SharePoint (up to 2017) it was the worst part of their day. The one thing their coworkers could agree on was that SharePoint is terrible and they'd rather use anything else.

A developer building a RAG integration for enterprise customers complains that SharePoint OAuth claims can't be scoped to particular sites or projects. Even with user login, they get access to all of a customer's SharePoint sites, including ones they don't want to index.

A longtime SharePoint admin says making it internet-facing has never been a good idea. When people wanted SharePoint as their 'web server', they set that installation up entirely separate from other instances on the network.

A user calls SharePoint one of the most bug-ridden programs they've worked with. A known bug with SolidWorks sporadically makes files impossible to open unless you edit metadata, and it has gone unfixed for years. Some features work only in the browser and some only in the app, with no documentation of which.

Opening SharePoint files in the browser goes through many SSO redirects and shows the files. Then, despite the user being fully authenticated, a 'sign in to see files' modal pops up, and clicking Cancel is the only way to interact with the files.

An enterprise admin calls SharePoint terrible software but says it's the only one that stands up under load and shards easily. In their view, open-source alternatives run fine in a homelab but likely fall over at enterprise scale.

A consultant says 9 of 10 Fortune 500 companies they work with use SharePoint. They argue many implementations are bad, but done right it's pretty solid. They see no better alternative short of maintaining 5-10 separate tools from multiple vendors.

After supporting SharePoint for two years, an admin called it an over-engineered mess that managers love and admins hate. It doesn't do what you'd expect but does a lot you don't need. They happily replaced it with several tools that together did the job properly.

By default, SharePoint search only indexed Office metadata, so documents couldn't be found unless everyone set metadata correctly, and saving from some Word versions could crash and lose work. The user built their own search index by crawling WebDAV, and the company used it for years instead.

One commenter says SharePoint is usable on a single server with a small workgroup. Beyond about two dozen people, it needs a server farm and becomes a full-time job, with frequent patches and an overly complicated restore-from-backup process.

At one workplace, SharePoint works well as a hybrid intranet and file share. Departments create simple content and attach documents, and sharing via Active Directory groups is simple. However, SharePoint lists used as an Access replacement often outgrow its limits and must be migrated to real systems.
One organization chose an Australian intranet product instead of SharePoint after being quoted upwards of $1 million for SharePoint licenses.
IT shut off Confluence on short notice and migrated all content to SharePoint. Five years of organized, easily searchable docs turned into a pile of Office documents and half-functioning 'pages'.

A Mac user finds SharePoint shows no hotkey tooltips, and documented shortcuts don't work with Ctrl or Cmd. They find Google Docs much faster thanks to more hotkeys and less clicking through nested dropdown menus.

A former intranet developer lists their SharePoint pain points:
- files in counterintuitive locations, found only through tribal knowledge
- years-old documents with no cleanup
- a complicated permission system
- major performance problems on data-heavy pages
- docs hidden because someone had them checked out

A former SharePoint admin who built workflows hated it, calling it bloated and complicated with documentation that's 'a cruel joke'. By contrast, they grew to like SQL Server, Visual Studio and PowerShell.

A current SharePoint admin doesn't find SharePoint too bad, setting aside PowerApps and Power Automate. Frequent users navigate it without fuss, but infrequent users waste a ridiculous amount of time hunting for non-obvious settings.

A non-developer loves SharePoint lists for getting colleagues to think about data more richly than spreadsheets. They create a site per project as a 'project-as-an-app' with constraints and workflows built with minimal effort. It's not without headaches, but they'd hate to lose it.

One user built many flows that log form data into lists, track submissions and move files, and found it very useful. Still, they struggle to understand SharePoint and rely on a well-organized bookmarks folder to avoid getting lost in the 'SharePoint maze'.
One user says modern SharePoint was rebuilt on React and is much improved since 2010. It's not a best-of-breed intranet, but if you already have M365 licenses, not using it is a waste.
